name: Arduino Uno R3
summary: A dependable starting point for prototyping interactive electronics. USB powered, beginner friendly, and ready for a thousand different ideas.
imageCredit: Photo: MakeMagazinDE, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: N20 Micro Gear Motor
summary: Compact geared motor for small robots, smart mechanisms, and mobile builds. A great balance of torque and speed in a tiny package.

name: 2S Li-ion Battery Pack
summary: A compact rechargeable power source for portable prototypes and robotics. Includes a protected pack with a standard JST lead.
safetyNote: Use a compatible charger and never short or puncture the battery pack.

name: HC-SR04 Ultrasonic
summary: Measures distance with sound, like a bat. The go-to sensor for obstacle-avoiding robots, parking sensors and water-level meters.
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)

name: ESP32 DevKit V1
summary: A powerful connected board for IoT projects. Built in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth make it a versatile choice for wireless prototypes.
imageCredit: Photo: Ubahnverleih, CC0 (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

name: SG90 Micro Servo
summary: A tiny, light servo you can turn to an exact angle. Ideal for robot arms, sensor scanners, door latches and RC models.
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)

name: Arduino Nano
summary: All the power of an Arduino UNO in a tiny board that plugs straight into a breadboard. Same ATmega328P chip, same code, much smaller.
imageCredit: Photo: MakeMagazinDE, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)

name: 65mm Rubber Wheel
summary: A grippy rubber tire on a lightweight hub, designed to pair with common TT gear motors for small robot chassis builds.

name: Raspberry Pi 5
imageCredit: Photo: SimonWaldherr, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A full desktop-class Linux computer the size of a credit card. Run Raspberry Pi OS, Python, a web server, a camera or an AI project, and control hardware through the 40-pin header.

specs.label: Processor
specs.value: Broadcom BCM2712, quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A76 @ 2.4 GHz

specs.label: Networking
specs.value: Gigabit Ethernet, dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0 / BLE

specs.label: Expansion
specs.value: 40-pin GPIO header, PCIe 2.0 x1, 2 × MIPI camera/display

safetyNote: Needs a good 5 V / 5 A USB-C supply; active cooling recommended under heavy load.

name: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
imageCredit: Photo: Laserlicht, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The popular, proven Raspberry Pi. A small Linux computer with dual 4K display output, Gigabit Ethernet and USB 3.0 for robotics, IoT hubs and learning to code.

specs.label: Networking
specs.value: Gigabit Ethernet, dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0 / BLE

specs.label: Expansion
specs.value: 40-pin GPIO header, MIPI CSI camera and DSI display ports

name: Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040)
imageCredit: Photo: Phiarc, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A tiny, low-cost microcontroller board from Raspberry Pi. Drag-and-drop programming over USB, with MicroPython or C/C++, and breadboard-friendly pins.

specs.label: Microcontroller
specs.value: RP2040, dual-core Arm Cortex-M0+ up to 133 MHz

specs.label: Interfaces
specs.value: 2 × UART, 2 × SPI, 2 × I2C, 16 PWM channels, 8 PIO state machines

safetyNote: 3.3 V logic: don't connect 5 V signals directly.

name: NodeMCU ESP8266 (LoLin V3)
imageCredit: Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A cheap Wi-Fi development board for IoT. Program it like an Arduino and connect sensors to your phone, a web dashboard or the cloud.

specs.label: Chip
specs.value: ESP8266EX, 32-bit Tensilica L106, 80 MHz (up to 160 MHz)

specs.label: I/O
specs.value: Digital pins D0–D8 with PWM, I2C, SPI, UART; 1 analog input (A0)

safetyNote: 3.3 V logic: don't connect 5 V signals directly.

name: ESP-01 Wi-Fi Module (ESP8266)
imageCredit: Photo: Make Magazin DE, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A thumbnail-sized ESP8266 Wi-Fi module. Add Wi-Fi to an Arduino using AT commands, or program it directly for very small IoT gadgets.

specs.label: Pins
specs.value: 8 (VCC, GND, TX, RX, CH_EN, RST, GPIO0, GPIO2)

safetyNote: 3.3 V only: powering it from 5 V will damage it. Use a 3.3 V regulator and level shifting.

name: RFID Reader Module RC522 (13.56 MHz)
imageCredit: Photo: Giacomo Alessandroni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Read and write contactless RFID cards and key tags. Build door locks, attendance systems and tap-to-start projects with an Arduino or ESP32.

specs.label: Reading distance
specs.value: Up to about 5 cm (depends on card and antenna)

safetyNote: Power from 3.3 V, not 5 V.

name: DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor Module
imageCredit: Photo: Edwiyanto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A simple, low-cost digital sensor for room temperature and humidity. Perfect for a first weather station or plant monitor.

name: DHT22 (AM2302) Temperature & Humidity Sensor Module
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The more accurate big brother of the DHT11, with a wider range and 0.1-step readings. Great when you need reliable climate data.

name: PIR Motion Sensor (HC-SR501)
imageCredit: Photo: Nowforever, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Detects people moving by sensing body heat. Use it for automatic lights, burglar alarms and motion-triggered cameras.

name: 16x2 Character LCD Display
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The classic text display. Show sensor readings, menus and messages on 2 lines of 16 characters with the Arduino LiquidCrystal library.

specs.label: Contrast
specs.value: Set with a 10 kΩ potentiometer on pin V0

safetyNote: Tip: an I2C backpack (PCF8574) cuts the wiring down to 4 wires.

name: 28BYJ-48 Stepper Motor + ULN2003 Driver
imageCredit: Photo: Kushagra Keshari, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A geared stepper motor that moves in precise small steps, with a plug-in driver board. Great for clocks, turntables, blinds and small CNC ideas.

specs.label: Driver
specs.value: ULN2003 Darlington array with 4 indicator LEDs

name: 5 V Single-Channel Relay Module
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Lets a small Arduino signal switch a much bigger load, like a lamp, fan or pump, using an electrically isolated mechanical switch.

specs.label: Contact rating
specs.value: 10 A 250 V AC / 10 A 30 V DC

specs.label: Control
specs.value: Digital signal from a microcontroller pin

safetyNote: Mains voltage can kill. Only switch mains with proper insulation and adult supervision.

name: TP4056 Li-ion Charger Module (with protection)
imageCredit: Photo: -stk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Charge a single 3.7 V Li-ion or LiPo cell, like an 18650, from any USB charger. The built-in protection stops overcharge, deep discharge and short circuits.

specs.label: Input
specs.value: 5 V via micro-USB or IN+/IN− pads

specs.label: Indicators
specs.value: Red LED charging, blue/green LED done

specs.label: Pads
specs.value: IN+, IN−, B+, B−, OUT+, OUT−

safetyNote: For one cell only (1S). Never leave charging Li-ion cells unattended.

name: Half-Size Breadboard (400 points)
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Build and change circuits without soldering. Push components and jumper wires into the holes and you're ready to test.

name: Female-to-Female Jumper Wires
imageCredit: Photo: Limor from New York City, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: Colour-coded wires with female sockets on both ends. Connect modules with pin headers, like sensors and drivers, straight to your board.

name: 5 mm Red LEDs
imageCredit: Photo: Nevit Dilmen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The first part of every electronics journey: blink an LED. Bright, cheap and perfect for indicators and learning.

specs.label: Polarity
specs.value: Long leg = anode (+), short leg = cathode (−)

safetyNote: Always use a series resistor (about 220–330 Ω at 5 V).

name: 10 kΩ Rotary Potentiometer
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A knob you can turn to change a value. Read it on an analog pin to control brightness, speed, volume or a menu.

specs.label: Mounting
specs.value: Panel mount with threaded bushing and nut

specs.label: Use
specs.value: Voltage divider into an analog input

name: EaglePower P60 KV330 Brushless Drone Motor
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A large brushless outrunner motor for heavy-lift multirotors, such as agricultural spraying drones. The speed controller (ESC) is built into the arm mount, so it fits straight onto a frame tube.

specs.label: Model / KV
specs.value: EaglePower P60, KV 330 rpm per volt (printed on the motor)

specs.label: Speed controller
specs.value: ESC built into the arm mount

specs.label: Mounting
specs.value: Clamps onto a round frame arm tube

safetyNote: High-power motor for large, high-voltage battery packs. Check the maker's spec sheet for the voltage, current and propeller before use. This is not the small 1000 KV motor used in the F450 Drone kit.

name: 35A Brushless ESC
imageCredit: Photo: Avsar Aras, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: An electronic speed controller (ESC) for driving a brushless motor from a LiPo battery. It takes a standard RC throttle signal from a receiver or flight controller and drives the motor's three phases.

specs.label: Leads
specs.value: Red/black battery leads, 3 motor-phase wires, 3-wire servo-style signal lead

safetyNote: One ESC is needed per motor. Match the ESC's current rating and supported cell count (S) to your motor and battery.

name: AGAPOWER 3S 11.1 V 5200 mAh 60C LiPo (Hard Case)
imageCredit: Photo: RC Lipo battery, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A high-capacity 3-cell lithium-polymer pack in a hard case, made for RC car racing. It also suits other projects that run on 3S (11.1 V) power.

specs.label: Connectors
specs.value: T-style (Deans-type) main plug and a balance lead, as pictured

safetyNote: LiPo safety: charge only with a LiPo balance charger, never unattended, and in a fire-safe bag. Don't over-discharge, puncture or use a swollen pack.

name: Zippy 2S 7.4 V 2200 mAh 20C LiPo
imageCredit: Photo: KundaliniZero, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A compact 2-cell LiPo pack. 7.4 V is a good fit for small RC cars, robot cars and projects that use a regulator for 5 V logic.
safetyNote: LiPo safety: charge only with a LiPo balance charger, never unattended, and in a fire-safe bag. Don't over-discharge, puncture or use a swollen pack.

name: 1S 3.7 V 1000 mAh LiPo Pouch Cell (063450)
imageCredit: Photo: BrittanyJ, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A thin, single-cell lithium-polymer pouch battery with wire leads. It powers wearables, ESP32 or Arduino projects and handheld gadgets, often with a TP4056 charger board.

specs.label: Size code
specs.value: 063450 (about 6 × 34 × 50 mm by the usual pouch-cell naming)

safetyNote: Use a charger made for single-cell Li-ion/LiPo (e.g. TP4056 with protection). Never puncture, bend or short the pouch.

name: Turnigy Accucel-6 LiPo Balance Charger
imageCredit: Photo: Teardown Central, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A popular hobby balance charger for LiPo, Li-ion and LiFe packs, plus NiMH/NiCd and lead-acid. It charges each cell evenly through the balance lead and has storage and discharge modes.

specs.label: Input
specs.value: 11–18 V DC (needs a separate power supply)

safetyNote: Power supply and leads may not be included. Always choose the correct battery type and cell count before charging.

name: 18650 & 21700 Li-ion Cells
imageCredit: Photo: Retired electrician, CC0 (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The two most common rechargeable cylindrical lithium-ion cells. 18650 powers most robot car kits and power banks; the larger 21700 holds more energy. Shown side by side for size.

specs.label: Capacity
specs.value: Depends on the cell model, check the cell's rating

goodFor: DIY battery packs with a BMS
safetyNote: Use a proper Li-ion charger and a battery holder or BMS. Never short, crush or heat the cells, and buy genuine cells from a trusted source.

name: CR2032 3 V Lithium Coin Cell
imageCredit: Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A standard non-rechargeable coin cell for RTC modules, remotes, small sensors and keeping a clock running when the main power is off.
safetyNote: Not rechargeable. Keep coin cells away from children: swallowing one can cause serious injury.

name: NEMA 17 Stepper Motor
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The stepper motor used in most 3D printers and small CNC machines. It moves in precise steps, so you can position things accurately without a feedback sensor. Drive it with an A4988 or a similar driver.

specs.label: Frame
specs.value: NEMA 17: about 42 × 42 mm square face (1.7 in)

specs.label: Mounting
specs.value: 4 × M3 holes on a 31 mm square, 22 mm pilot boss

specs.label: Step angle
specs.value: Commonly 1.8° (200 steps per revolution), check the motor's label

safetyNote: Needs a stepper driver (e.g. A4988). Set the driver's current limit to match the motor.

name: A4988 Stepper Motor Driver Module
imageCredit: Photo: Kushagra Keshari, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A small driver board that lets an Arduino or ESP32 drive a bipolar stepper motor (such as a NEMA 17) with just two pins, STEP and DIR. It has adjustable current limiting.

specs.label: Current
specs.value: About 1 A per coil without cooling, up to 2 A per coil with a heatsink and airflow

safetyNote: Set the current limit with the trimpot before use. Never connect or disconnect the motor while powered. Add a ≥47 µF capacitor across the motor supply. The board can get very hot.

name: Standard-Size Hobby Servo
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A full-size RC servo for jobs that need more strength than a micro SG90, such as steering, robot arm joints and grippers. It turns to an angle set by a PWM signal.

specs.label: Control
specs.value: 50 Hz PWM, about 1–2 ms pulse sets the angle

specs.label: Supply
specs.value: Typically 4.8–6 V, check the servo's rating

safetyNote: Power servos from a separate supply that can deliver enough current, not the Arduino's 5 V pin. Connect the grounds together.

name: Continuous Rotation Servo
imageCredit: Photo: oomlout, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A servo modified to spin continuously in either direction instead of moving to an angle. It makes an easy, geared drive motor for small robots with no separate motor driver needed.

specs.label: Control
specs.value: PWM pulse width sets speed and direction; about 1.5 ms = stop

specs.label: Supply
specs.value: Typically 4.8–6 V, check the servo's rating

safetyNote: If it creeps at the stop signal, adjust the trim or calibrate the stop pulse in code.

name: 130-Size DC Hobby Motor
imageCredit: Photo: Nevit Dilmen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The classic small DC motor found in toys, fans and school science kits. Wire it to a battery and it spins, or use a transistor or motor driver for speed control.

specs.label: Frame
specs.value: 130 size: flat-sided can, about 20 × 15 mm, about 25 mm long

specs.label: Voltage
specs.value: Typically 3–6 V for hobby 130 motors, check the seller's rating

safetyNote: Add a 0.1 µF capacitor across the tabs to reduce electrical noise. Use a transistor or motor driver, not a microcontroller pin directly.

name: Coreless Micro DC Motor (3.7 V)
imageCredit: Photo: Armenak Margarian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A tiny, high-speed coreless motor that runs on a single 3.7 V LiPo cell. These are the motors used in micro quadcopters and small, light projects.
safetyNote: Micro-drone motors usually come in clockwise and counter-clockwise versions, and the wire colours often mark which is which. Check the seller's info.

name: Vibration Motor (ERM)
imageCredit: Photo: Majid (Wikimedia Commons user), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A small DC motor with an off-centre weight on its shaft. When it spins, it shakes, which is how phones, game controllers and alarms buzz.

specs.label: Type
specs.value: Eccentric rotating mass (ERM) brushed DC motor

specs.label: Effect
specs.value: Vibration strength rises with voltage and speed

safetyNote: Drive it through a transistor (with a flyback diode), not straight from a microcontroller pin.

name: BO Motor Wheel (Pair)
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: The plastic wheels with rubber tyres used on most Arduino robot car kits. They push straight onto the shaft of yellow BO (TT) gear motors.

specs.label: Fits
specs.value: BO / TT gear motor output shaft

name: Track Belt Wheel Set (Tank Chassis)
imageCredit: Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (background removed)
summary: A set of rubber track belts and drive wheels for building a tracked, tank-style robot. Tracks grip better than wheels on rough ground, carpet and ramps.

specs.label: Contents
specs.value: 4 drive/idler wheels and 2 rubber track belts, as pictured

specs.label: Use
specs.value: Small hobby and robotics tank chassis

safetyNote: Motors, frame and mounting hardware are not included.
